opus-5.5.text:
Ha, well, I'd want to be careful with a claim like that. I think it's probably a little exaggerated, and in any case it's not really a statement about me being especially clever. It's more a statement about what I chose to spend my time on.

For a long stretch, especially in the adversarial examples era, a huge number of papers proposed defenses, and very few people were seriously trying to break them. Breaking defenses wasn't seen as glamorous. You don't get a shiny new method out of it. So when you're one of a small number of people willing to sit down and carefully attack defense after defense, you end up with a long list fairly quickly. That says more about how lopsided the incentives were than about any individual.

The other honest point is that a lot of these defenses weren't that hard to break once you looked carefully. Many of them failed for the same few reasons. Gradient masking, evaluating against the wrong threat model, or not adapting the attack to the specific defense. Once you've seen that pattern a dozen times, you start recognizing it almost immediately. It's less "brilliant attack" and more "did anyone actually try the obvious adaptive attack?"

And of course I didn't do most of this alone. Many of these papers had wonderful collaborators: Anish Athalye, David Wagner, Florian Tramèr, and lots of others. So attributing the count to one person isn't quite right.

What I'd actually like people to take away isn't the number. It's that evaluating defenses properly is hard, it's undervalued, and the field is much better off when more people do it. If someone else came along and broke more defenses than me, I'd be thrilled. That would mean the community is taking evaluation seriously, which matters a lot more now that these systems are actually deployed.

r002.rationale: It says few researchers were trying to break defenses and Carlini spent time doing so, but does not say he got to the defenses before other researchers did.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back on it a bit, honestly. I think the claim is a little misleading, because the way the count works out, a lot of what I've done is just repeatedly breaking the same kind of thing over and over. If you count papers, sure, I've written a lot of papers that say "here is a defense, and here is why it doesn't work." But the number is high in part because the field kept producing defenses that failed in very similar ways, and once you know the pattern, breaking the next one is often a few days of work rather than a new research idea.

The other thing I'd say is that it's not really a measure of me being especially clever. It's much more a statement about how hard evaluation is. When you propose a defense, you're in this uncomfortable position where you have to argue a negative: that no attack exists. And people are naturally optimistic about their own work. They try the standard attacks, the attacks don't work, and they conclude the defense is good. What they usually haven't done is sit down as an adversary and ask, "if I actually wanted to break this specific thing, knowing everything about how it's built, what would I do?" That mindset is the whole trick. It's less about having some secret technique and more about being willing to spend the time, being genuinely skeptical of a result even when it looks good, and not stopping when the first few attempts fail.

And I should say, I've been wrong plenty of times too. There are defenses I thought I'd break quickly and couldn't, and there are evaluation mistakes I've made myself. So I'd rather people take away the lesson that the bar for claiming robustness should be very high, than that there's some person out there who's unusually good at breaking things. The honest version of the claim is that the field has, for a long time, had a very low bar for what counts as evidence that a defense works, and someone just needed to keep pointing that out.

astra-6.text: I don’t know that I’d make that claim. There are a lot of people doing very good work in this space, and I wouldn’t know how to count it. But I have spent a lot of time breaking defenses, and one thing that makes that possible is that breaking a defense is often much easier than building one. The person building it has to account for every possible attack. I only have to find one thing they missed. So if I’ve broken a lot of defenses, I think that says as much about the difficulty of the problem as it does about me.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t know that I’d make that claim. It’s very hard to count these things. If someone puts up a defense and I find ten ways around it, is that ten breaks or one? And there are a lot of people doing really good work here.

What I would say is that I’ve spent a lot of time trying to break defenses, and the thing you learn is that getting an attack to fail is very different from showing that a defense works. An attack can fail because the defense is strong, but it can also fail because you weren’t trying hard enough or weren’t asking the right question. A lot of my work is about figuring out which of those is happening.
